title: Merlin's New Zealand Retreat Is Less About Geography and More About Where Cockpit Autonomy Software Actually Scales
summary: Merlin's September 9 withdrawal from its New Zealand small-aircraft STC bid — and its pivot toward large commercial and military transports — reveals a strategic logic that goes well beyond which aircraft type it's targeting.
body_markdown:
This is an update to a story I covered back in July, when Merlin's autonomous Caravan landing at Oshkosh read as a compelling demonstration that the certification path was moving. A lot has changed since then.

<cite index="41-1">On September 9, Merlin, Inc. announced plans to pursue a civil certification strategy that sets it on a path to bring autonomy to large aircraft.</cite> The headline framing was about ambition — 7,000 commercial transports, a looming pilot shortage — but the more revealing detail was buried underneath: <cite index="41-3">to concentrate its efforts on large aircraft, the company is withdrawing its small aircraft Supplemental Type Certificate application with the Civil Aviation Authority of New Zealand, and will apply the technical foundation and regulatory experience it built there to the new program.</cite>

That's not a pivot. That's a full reset of the certification strategy.

## The Real Signal Isn't the Target Market — It's the Certification Logic

Small aircraft STC work and large aircraft type certification are not the same regulatory exercise done at different scales. They involve different FAA offices, different software assurance standards, different levels of scrutiny on AI and ML systems, and fundamentally different risk tolerances from the certification authority. What Merlin is really announcing is that it's abandoning one certification playbook and betting its future on a harder one.

The strategic rationale they've laid out leans heavily on the defense side: <cite index="43-7">the company plans a phased approach to certifying its Merlin Pilot autonomy system on large, high-assurance aircraft, leveraging experience from its New Zealand program and its C-130J autonomy work with U.S. Special Operations Command.</cite> And the regulatory artifacts from New Zealand aren't being discarded — <cite index="43-8">Merlin's New Zealand certification work achieved SOI 3 and a Stage 4 issue paper on AI/ML-based natural language processing, which will inform future collaboration with the FAA and other regulators.</cite> That's a meaningful data point: they're carrying forward IP and regulatory paperwork, not starting from zero.

But the certification gap between where they are and where they're going is substantial, and the regulatory environment is actively working against the endpoint they've described. <cite index="37-8,37-9,37-10">EASA, which also prohibits single-pilot operations in commercial airliners, recently performed a study on eMCO and concluded that it would be unsafe with current cockpit technologies — this was particularly notable because Airbus was pushing for eMCO with its upcoming A350F freighter — and EASA has shut the door on this for now, instead pivoting focus on boosting safety in existing two-pilot cockpits.</cite> I covered the EASA eMCO delay in depth back in August, and that regulatory signal hasn't softened since.

## The Pilot Shortage Argument Is Real, But It's Not a Certification Argument

<cite index="37-6">Merlin has specifically called out that there are over 7,000 large commercial transports in the US, and that the country could be short of over 30,000 pilots by 2032.</cite> That workforce math is genuine and the addressable market framing is understandable — but it conflates a demand signal with a regulatory pathway. The FAA and EASA don't accelerate certification timelines because an industry is short-staffed. They might accelerate standard-setting conversations, but the assurance requirements on AI in a transport-category cockpit don't bend because of a hiring crisis.

What the pilot shortage argument actually does is strengthen the case for a different category of cockpit software: not full autonomy, but AI co-pilot assistance tools that reduce single-pilot workload within existing two-crew regulatory frameworks. That's a nearer-term market, and it's the one where Merlin's New Zealand experience — specifically the NLP work that reached Stage 4 issue paper status — could actually matter in a commercial timeline that airlines can plan around.

<cite index="37-12">Merlin and its autonomous systems won't result in crew size reductions for the foreseeable future.</cite> That's a fair assessment of where things stand. The more interesting question, to me, is whether Merlin's software stack — built for a high-assurance military environment — can find a commercial expression in the cockpit assistance layer that doesn't require the autonomy endpoint at all. The defense-to-commercial translation story is often more complicated than the press release suggests, but the regulatory artifacts they're carrying forward are worth watching.

email_brief: Merlin, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRLN) announced on September 9, 2026 that it's withdrawing its small-aircraft STC application with New Zealand's CAANZ and pivoting its civil certification strategy to large commercial and military transport aircraft, citing a US fleet of 7,000+ large transports and a projected pilot shortage of 30,000+ by 2032. The pivot comes against a difficult regulatory backdrop — EASA recently concluded that eMCO (single-pilot commercial operations) is unsafe with current cockpit technology, effectively closing the near-term door on the crew-reduction endpoint Merlin's autonomy pitch implies. The story matters right now because it crystallizes the tension between cockpit AI ambition and what certification authorities will actually approve, and raises the question of whether Merlin's most viable commercial path is actually the nearer-term AI assistance layer — not full autonomy — within existing two-crew frameworks.
